WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS  
Penalty in dowry death cases  
*41. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be 
pleased to state:  
(a) the reasons behind the Law Commission's recommendat ion not to prescribe 
capital punishment in dowry death cases; 
(b) whether the Commission's recommendations are bindin g on Government or 
are only persuasive in nature; and 
(c) what would be the legal position in case the dowry death falls within the ambit of 
offence of murder? 
THE  MINISTER  OF   LAW  AND   JUSTICE   (SHRI  H.   R.   
BHARDWAJ):  
i) The Law Commission in its 202nd Report on "Propo sal to amend Section 304-B 
of Indian penal Code" (available on the website-htt p://Iawcornmissionofindia.nic.in ) 
has opined that there is no warrant for prescribing death sentence for the offence of 
dowry death as defined in  

2    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]                   Starred Questions  
Section 304-B of Indian Penal Code having regard to  presumptive character of the 
offence, absence of direct connection between the d eath and the offender and the 
gravity of culpable conduct as well as the object s ought to be achieved thereby. 
Further, there is distinction between Section 302 (Murder) and Section 304-B (dowry 
death) of the IPC. If charge is framed under Sectio n 304-B, but after recording and 
appreciation of evidence, the case proved to be a c ase under Section 302, the charge 
can be altered and the accused can very well be punished under Section 302 and if the 
court finds that the case under Section 302 to be a rarest of rare cases, then the offender 
can very well be awarded with capital punishment.  
(b) The Commission's recommendations are not binding on  the Government and 
are only recommendatory/advisory in nature. 
(c) If the case of dowry death falls within the ambit of offence of murder, then the 
competent court can award punishment under Section 302 of IPC. 
Policy for non-conventional energy schemes  
*42 SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY: Will the Minister of NE W AND 
RENEWABLE ENERGY be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government have formulated any non-conventional energy policy in the 
country; 
(b) if so, the details and the features thereof and the  role of such policy in rural, 
tribal and remote areas of the country; 
(c) whether this policy is being implemented in the country; 
(d)if so, the details of funds allocated, released and actually spent on 
implementation of various projects in rural areas o f the country during the last three 
years, till date, project-wise, State-wise and year-wise; and 
(e) the details of non-conventional energy sources which are operational at present, 
alongwith the potential sources for the same, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NEW AND 
RENEWABLE ENERGY (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) and (b ) No, Sir. 
However, an Expert Committee constituted by the Pla nning Commission has 
prepared an Integrated Energy Policy Report (IEPR) covering all sources of energy 
including renewable energy sources. This report has  highlighted the need to 
maximally develop domestic supply options and diver sify energy sources. It has 
also projected that renewables may account for 5 to 6 per cent of India's energy mix 
by 2031-32 and has observed that the distributed na ture of renewables can provide 
many socio-economic benefits for the country, inclu ding its rural, tribal and remote 
areas.  
(c) The recommendations of the IEPR are yet to be a ccepted by the Government. 
Meanwhile, the Ministry has proposed an outlay of Rs. 10,460 crore for the 11 th Plan 
period for development of new and renewable energy in the country.  
(d) State-wise details of the central financial ass istance provided by the Ministry 
under various renewable energy schemes/programmes during the last three years, viz., 
2004-05,2005-06, 2006-07 are given in Statement-I. (See below)  
(e) The renewable energy sources exploited so far in the country are solar, wind, 
small hydro and bio energy. Details of their estima ted potential and cumulative 
achievements as on 30.9.2007 under different programmes are given in Statement-H 
(See below) State-wise details of the cumulative achieve ments are given in 
Statement-Ill.

NOTE :—  
(1) although the potential is based on surplus agro-res idues, in practice there 
are several barriers in collection and transportati on of such agro-residues 
to the generation site and biomass power generation  units prefer to use 
fuel-wood for techno-economic reasons. A potential of 45,000 MWe from 
around 20mha of wastelands assumed to be yielding 1 0MT/ha/annum of 
woody biomass having 4000 k-cal/kg with system effi ciency of 30% and 
75% PLF has not been taken into account. In order t o realize this potential 
a major inter-Ministerial initiative involving, amo ng others, Environment 
& Forests, Agriculture, Rural Development, and Panc hayati Raj would be 
required. Further, a Biomass Atlas is under prepara tion which is expected 
to more accurately assess state-wise renewable ener gy potential from agro-
residues. 
(2) Potential based on areas having wind power density (wpd) greater than 200 
W/m 2 assuming land availability in potential areas @ 1 p er cent and 
requirement of wind farms @ 12 ha/MW, not all of wh ich may be 
technically feasible and economically viable for gr id-interactive wind 
power. In line with international practice for sett ing up grid-interactive 
wind power systems on sites having wpd greater than  300W/m 2, potential 
would be 5000 MW. Further, preliminary surveys do n ot at this juncture 
suggest a sizeable grid-interactive offshore wind power potential. 
(3) Technically feasible and economically viable hydro potential is generally 
accepted at 40% of the total estimated potential. A ccordingly, the 
technically feasible and economically viable small hydropower potential 
could be around 6000MW. 
(4) With the establishment of new sugar mills and moder nization of existing 
ones, technically feasible potential is assessed at  5000 MWe, not all of 
which may be economically viable. Furthermore, seve ral sugar 
companies/cooperatives are unable to develop bankab le projects on 
account of their financial and liquidity positions. 
(5) With expansion of urban population post census 2001 , current technically 
feasible municipal waste-to-energy potential is assessed at 1700 MWe, not 
all of which may be economically viable. However, s ubsidy disbursement 
under the municipal waste to energy programme had been kept in abeyance 
on the orders of the Supreme Court in the case of a  PIL, in May 2005. This 
stay has been vacated in May 2007 for setting up 5 pilot projects for the 
time being. 
(6) Not all of this renewable energy potential may be s uitable for grid-
interactive power for technical and/or economic rea sons. Further, estimate 
excludes potential for solar power, which is depend ent on future 
developments that might make solar technology cost- competitive for grid-
interactive power generation applications.

data-base of professors and scientists with expertise in instrumentation, who

(viii) Technology Parks and 'Incubation centres' in proximity to R&D institutions

(ix) The Government may set up a few component and subsystem development 
technology parks.

Delay  in  pronouncing judgements  
*51. SHRI VARINDER SINGH BAJWA: Will the Minister o f LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government have taken note of the serio us delays caused by the 
members of higher judiciary in the country by sitti ng over orders for years after 
having completed the hearings in the matters;  
(b) if so, whether Government proposed to solve thi s problem through 
legislation or directions and guidelines;  
(c) if so, by when that is likely to be done; and 
(d) if not, how Government propose to solve this problem? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ ): (a) to 
(d) Government is aware that in some cases in the H igh Courts there may be 
unusual delay in pronouncing judgements after heari ngs have been completed. The 
matter, however, is an internal working of the judi ciary and the various High Courts 
have their own rules and procedures on such issues. The Supreme Court of India has 
considered the issue of delay in pronouncing judgem ents and unexplained long 
interval between conclusion of arguments and delive ry of judgements and given 
detailed guidelines regarding expeditious pronouncement of judgements. In Criminal 
Appeals No. 3 89 of 1998 in the case of Anil Rai vs. State of Bihar with Criminal 
Appeals No. 387-88 of 1998 in the case of Subash Chand Rai and another vs. State of 
Bihar with Criminal Appeal No. 199 of 1999 in the c ase of Awani Rai vs State of 
Bihar, decided on August 6,2001, the Supreme Court framed the followed 
guidelines'to be followed by the High Court.  
(i) The Chief Justices of the High Courts may issue s appropriate directions to 
the Registry that in a case where the judgement is reserved and is 
pronounced later, a column be added in the judgemen t where, on the first 
page, after the cause-title, date of reserving the judgement and date of 
pronouncing it be separately mentioned by the Court Officer concerned. 
(ii) That Chief Justices of the High Courts, on the ir administrative side, should 
direct the Court officers/Readers of the various Be nches in the High 
Courts to furnish every month the list of the cases  in the matter where the 
judgements reserved are not pronounced within the period of that month.  
(iii) On noticing that after conclusion of the argu ments the judgement is not 
pronounced within a period of two months the Chief Justice concerned 
shall draw the attention of the Bench concerned to the pending matter of 
such cases in which the judgements have not been pr onounced within a 
period of six weeks from the date of conclusion of the arguments amongst 
the Judges of the High Court of their information. Such communication be 
conveyed as confidential and in a sealed cover.  
(iv) Where a judgment is not prouounced within thre e months from the date of 
reserving judgement, any of the parties in the case  is permitted to file an 
application in the High Court with a prayer for ear ly judgement. Such 
application, as and when filed, shall be listed bef ore the Bench concerned 
within two days excluding the intervening holidays. 
(v) If the judgement, for any reason, is not pronou nced within a period of six 
months, any of the parties shall be entitled to mov e an application before 
the Chief Justice of the High Court with prayer to withdraw the said case 
and to make it over to any  

Written Answers to  [19 NOV. 2007]            Starred Questions    19  
other Bench for fresh arguments. It is open to the Chief Justice to grant the 
said prayer or to pass any other order as he deems fit in the circumstances.

(a) is it correct that India still has the largest number of illiterates in the world and 
according to the 2001 census, India had nearly 304 million illiterate people, aged 
seven plus, and with its poor literacy level, India  ranks a poor 126th in the Human 
Development Index of UNDP;

SINGH), (a) and (b) In the past decades, there had been a continuous increase in 
India in the absolute number of illiterates, despit e the increase in the literacy rate.

to 304.11 million from 328.88 million in the year 1991, which works out to reduction 
in illiteracy from 47.8% of the population in 1991 to 35.2% in 2001.  
As per Human Development Report 2006, India ranks 1 26th out of  the 177 
countries of the world covered by this Report. Adul t literacy is only one of  the 
several variables on the basis of which the Human Development Index is calculated. 
It would not be correct to say that the illiteracy rate has not been reduced despite 
major schemes such as the National Literacy Mission  (NLM) and Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan (SSA). The decline in the number/percentage  of  the illiterate persons as 
noted above, can be attributed largely to the activ ities under Elementary Education 
and Adult Education. Under SSA, which commenced in 2001, substantially larger 
enrolment of children has been recorded as also a fall in the number of out-of-school 
children.

contribute to the persistence of  the illiteracy in the country.

28    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]               Unstarred Questions  
(c) by when this system is proposed to be set up; and 
(d) whether it would find out the earthquakes from the atmospheric and ocean 
current? 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) Yes, 
Sir. India Meteorological Department (IMD) has commissioned a system to monitor 
earthquakes within and outside the country for all significant earthquakes, which 
affect India. The system consists of different type s of observatories spread all over 
the country. Data from 40 stations are electronical ly collected and transmitted to 
central processing unit at New Delhi for accurate e stimation of location of the 
earthquake (epicenter), time of occurrence and magn itude (size) of the earthquake. 
The estimation of intensity over a wider affected a rea around the epicenter is done 
through post earthquake surveys.  
(c) Additional in the aftermath of the Great Sumatra Ea rthquake of 26th 
December, 2004, Ministry of Earth Sciences has set up an Early Warning System 
for Tsunamis at the Indian National Centre for Ocea n Information Services 
(INCOIS), Hyderabad. As part of this, a most modern  real time seismic monitoring 
network has been made operational with four field s tations at Bhuj, Hyderabad, 
Chennai and Shillong and two Central Receiving Stat ions at Hyderabad and New 
Delhi already functional. Installation of 13 more s tations is in progress. The system 
has facilities for real time data transmission from  field stations and automatic 
estimation of location, time of occurrence and magnitude of the earthquake over the 
north Indian Ocean zone. 
(d) The new system does not depend upon observations of  atmosphere or ocean 
current for detecting the earthquakes. It is based on sensors for detecting very small 
displacements of the ground during earthquakes. How ever, instrumentation 
commissioned over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian  Sea as a part of Tsunami 
Early Warning System measures/monitors sea level ch anges, sea bottom pressure 
changes, wave amplitudes and tides in real time following earthquake occurrence in the 
north Indian Ocean.

†119. SHRI JAI PARKASH AGGARWAL: Will the Minister of LAW AND

interdepartmental co-operation conference organized  in Delhi in August, 2006, 
expressed concern over lack of honesty in some sect ions of judiciary and emphasized

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI 
K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Hon'ble Prime Minister, in his address to the 
National Meet on Social Justice and Legal Empowerment held on August 19,2006 has 
inter-alia observed as follows:  
"....there are concerns often voiced in various quarters about the delays in disposal of 
cases and the consequent backlog that has built up over the years. There is 
concern about the cost of litigation and the cost o f obtaining justice. There is 
growing concern also about probity—or the lack of i t-in some sections of the 
judiciary. I have said this before, and I say this again, that we take great pride in 
the quality and effectiveness of our judicial syste m. But in the larger scheme of 
governance, it is incumbent upon any healthy instit ution to continue to reflect 
from time to time on its role, on the expectations from it and on the scope for 
improvement. This will help us take steps to improv e our performance and to 
meet the fast changing needs of the times that we live in. Above all, it will make 
our justice delivery system more sensitive to the n eeds of the poorest of our 
people. Especially those who are most discriminated against in our society."  
Allegations of deviant behaviour involving acts of corruption and moral turpitude 
against some Judges of High Courts and some members of Judicial Service of the States 
have come to the notice of the Government. The Chief Justice of a High Court has the 
competence to receive and look into complaints agai nst the conduct of a Judge of his

members of Judicial Service of a State, under article 235 of the Constitution of India, 
the administrative and disciplinary control over the members

Solar energy generation  
129. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of NEW A ND RENEWABLE 
ENERGY be pleased to state:  
(a) the quantum of solar energy generated in the country as on date; 
(b) whether Government propose to give priority to solar energy over hydro power 
and thermal power; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) the funds allocated to each State during the last three years, to popularize solar 
energy; and 
(e) the details of manufacturers/suppliers of solar energy system in each State as on 
date? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NEW AND RENEWABLE 
ENERGY (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) to (c) India rec eives solar energy 
equivalent to over 5,000 trillion kWh per year. The daily average solar energy incident over 
India varies from 4-7 kWh per square metre depending upon the location. Solar energy can 
be harnessed through two routes, namely solar photovoltaic (PV) and solar thermal, by 
direct conversion to electricity and heat energy respectively.  
The utilization of solar energy in the country is regularly increasing, however, the 
high initial cost of the solar energy systems is a barrier in its large-scale utilization. The 
estimated unit cost of electricity from grid connected solar energy plant is estimated 
to be around Rs. 12-15 per unit, which is very high compared to electricity generated 
from conventional sources including thermal power a nd other renewable energy 
sources such as wind, small hydro and biomass.  
A total of 33 grid interactive solar photovoltaic power plants have been installed in 
the country with financial assistance from the Ministry. These plants, with aggregate 
capacity of 2.125 megawatt peak (MWp), are estimated to generate about 2.5 million 
units of electricity in a year.  
In view of the high initial cost, at present solar energy systems are mainly being used 
for stand-alone applications, in lighting, telecommunication, small power requirements, 
battery charging, water heating and cooking etc. so far around 14 lakh solar photovoltaic 
systems aggregating to about 110 Megawatt peak solar photovoltaic module capacity have 
been installed in the country. In addition about 6 lakh solar cookers and about 20 lakh 
square metre collector area has been installed for solar water heating applications, which 
is equivalent to about 1400 Megawatt thermal capacity.  
(d) The details of State-wise release of funds during the last three years for various 
solar energy programmes are given in Statement-I (see below). 
(e) The State-wise details of manufacturers of solar photovoltaic cells/modules, solar 
cookers, flat plate solar thermal collector based water heating systems and suppliers of 
evacuated tube collector based water heating systems are given in the Statement-II.

Criteria for defining creamy layer  
151. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of SOCI AL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state:  
(a) the criteria for placing a person within the creamy  layer in different States, in 
the case of OBCs, State-wise; 
(b) whether the OBCs falling under the category of crea my layer are not allowed 
the benefit of reservation; and 
(c) whether Government have any guidelines for States, for determining the creamy 
layer and if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUS TICE AND 
EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI SUBBULAKSHMI JAGADEESAN): (a)  to (c) 
The creamy layer has been defined vide Government of India Office Memorandum 
(OM) No. 36012/22/93-Estt. (SCT) dated 8th September, 1993 as amended vide OM 
No. 36033/3/2004-Estt. (Res) dated 9th March, 2004.  As per these, children of 
certain categories of persons holding constitutiona l posts, Officers of certain 
categories of persons working in the Central/State Governments, Public Sector 
Undertakings, Armed Forces including Para Military Forces, Professional class and 
those engaged in Trade and Industry, certain proper ty owners etc. and the persons 
having gross annual income of Rs. 2.5 lakh or above  possessing wealth above the 
exemption limit as prescribed in the Wealth Tax Act for a period of three consecutive 
years fall in creamy layer. OBCs falling under the category of creamy layer are not 
allowed the benefit of reservation. The State Gover nments are free to fix their own 
criteria for purpose of the State List.  
In pursuance of the judgment of Supreme Court deliv ered in 1992 in Indira 
Sawhney & Others Vs. Union of India & Others case, Central Government and all 
the State Governments/ Union Territories set up the ir own Commissions for 
identification of Castes/Communities for inclusion in the Central/State lists. The 
judgment also mentioned that it shall be open to th e Government of India and 
respective State Governments to device the procedur es/methods to be followed by 
such bodies.  
So far as the criteria for placing a person within the creamy layer in different 
States is concerned, it is at the discretion of the State Governments.

Scheduled Tribes are notified by the Presidential Order under Article 342 (1) of the 
Constitution. State-wise list of notified Scheduled  Tribes in India is indicated in the 
Annual Report 2006-07 of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, copies of which are available 
in the Parliament Library. The criteria followed by  Government of India for 
identification of communities for inclusion in the list of Scheduled Tribes are as 
follows:  
(i)  Indication of primitive traits;  
(ii)  Distinctive culture;  
(iii)  Geographical isolation;  
(iv)  Shyness of contact with the community at large; and 
(v)  Backwardness.  
(d) No formal proposal for inclusion of Nepali lang uage speaking sub-castes in 
the list of Scheduled Tribes has been received from  any State Govemment/UT 
Administration so far.

Details of steps taken by the Government to implement the guidelines laid down by the

* The Government has requested all the Central Minist ries/Departments, 
Chief Secretaries of all the State Governments/Unio n Territory 
Administrations, Universities/ Institutions, Centra l Board of Secondary 
Education, All India Council of Technical Education  to constitute 
complaints committees and to ensure that the guidel ines laid down by the 
Supreme Court in the Vishaka case for prevention of  sexual harassment at 
workplace are implemented.  
* The National Commission for Women (NCW) formulated a Code of 
Conduct for Workplace, putting down the Supreme Cou rt's guidelines 
mentioned above in a simple manner. This has been c irculated to State 
Commissions for Women, Non-Governmental Organisations, the apex bodies 
of the Corporate Sector, Public Sector undertakings , Media, 
Ministries/Departments and other institutions. 
* The NCW has instituted a series of interactive meet ings with Public 
Sector Undertakings/Banks/Universities/Educational 
Institutions/Hotels/Media etc. to assess the extent of implementation of the 
guidelines. 
* Department of Public Enterprises issued circular in  May, 1998 to all 
administrative Ministries/Departments concerned with Central Public Sector 
Establishments to direct the Chief Executives of CP SEs under their 
administrative control for adherence and compliance of the Supreme Court's 
guidelines on prevention of sexual harassment by ma king amendments in 
the CDA Rules of the CPSEs. 
* So far as implementation of the Supreme Court guide lines in regard to 
setting up of complaint committee in small establishments like shops and call 
centres are concerned section 1(3) of the Industrial Employment (Standing 
Orders) Act, 1947 applies to every establishment wh erein 100 and more 
workers are employed. However, appropriate Governme nt may apply the 
provisions of the Act to any industrial establishme nt employing less than 
100 persons. Since the State Governments are the ap propriate Government 
in respect of commercial establishments like shops and call centres, 
necessary instructions have been issued by the Mini stry of Labour and 
Employment during January, 2005 to all Labour Secretaries asking them to 
take suitable action to apply the provisions of the  Industrial Employment 
(Standing Orders) Act, 1946 to small establishments  like call centres and 
shops in the unorganized sector.

during July, 2004 to provide that the Complaints Committee established in 
each Ministry or Department or Office for inquiring  into complaints of 
sexual harassment shall be deemed to be the inquiry  authority appointed 
by the disciplinary authority and the Complaints Co mmittee shall hold the

proceedings for award of a major penalty).

Khurda-Bolangir Rail Line  
*21.   MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA:  
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government are aware that the inordinate de lay in construction of 
Khurda-Bolangir rail link, sanctioned in 1994-95, h as triggered severe public 
resentment in Orissa State; 
(b) whether the MPs and MLAs of the area have impressed  upon him for 
allotment of adequate funds for completion of this project within a time-bound 
period; and 
(c) if so, what is the status of this project, indicating the time-frame within which 
it would be completed? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) As  per the 
information available, on such public resentment ha s come to the notice of the 
Government.  
(b) Yes, Sir. Demands have been received from State Gov ernment of Orissa and 
elected representatives in this regard. 
(c) Land acquisition has been taken up and so far, about 900 acres out of 4951 acres 
has been acquired. Earthwork, bridges etc. taken up from km. 0 to 36. An expenditure 
of Rs. 67.83 crore was incurred upto 31.03.2007 and  an outlay of Rs. 20 crore has 
been provided for 2007-08. No target date for completion has been fixed yet. The work 
is being progressed as per the availability of resources. 
Halting of Trains at Yerraguntla Station  
*22.    SHRI NANDIYELLAIAH: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS b e pleased 
to state:  
(a) whether Government of Andhra Pradesh had requested his Ministry to provide 
haltage of Kachiguda-Chennai Egmore Express, Nizamu ddin-Tirupathi Sampark 
Express and Mumbai-Madurai Lokmanya Tilak Express a t Yerraguntla railway 
station; and 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir, in 
response to the requests received from the Governme nt and the Members of 
Parliament from Andhra Pradesh, stoppage of 6751/67 52 Kacheguda-Chennai 
Egmore Express at Yerraguntla has been provided fro m 01.10.2007 on an 
experimental basis for six months. However, stoppag es of 2707/2708 Nizamuddin-
Tirupati Andhra Pradesh Samapark Kranti Express and  1043/1044 Madurai 
Lokmanya Tilak(T) Express at Yerraguntla station as requested have been examined 
and not found feasible at present, due to lack of commercial justification.  
Vacancies in railways  
*23.  SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
RAILWAYS be pleased to state:  
(a) whether it is a fact that the railways is not f illing up vacancies in various 
categories;

(c) if not, the vacancies filled during the last three years; and

earliest?  
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) 98,343 (ninety eight thousand three hundred forty three) vacancies were filled 
up on the railways during last three years. 
(d) Occurrence and filling up of vacancies is a continu ous process. While a few 
vacancies are likely to exist in this continuous pr ocess at any point of time, the 
policy of the Government is to fill up the vacancie s promptly as per procedure. 
General Managers are empowered to assess the requir ement and get the same 
filled up from time to time by placing indents on R ailway Recruitment Boards 
(RRBs) in case of Group 'C categories. For Group 'D' requirement and recruitment is 
done by Railways themselves. The vacancies to be fi lled up have to be given wide 
publicity in conformity with the Constitutional pro visions and guidelines issued by 
the Department of Personnel & Training pursuant to directive of Hon'ble Supreme 
Court of India.

Stampede at Mughalsarai station  
*25.    SHRI VARINDER SINGH BAJWA:  
           SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR:  
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state:  
(a) the number of persons who lost their lives and were seriously injured due to a 
stampede at Mughalsarai railway station on the 3rd October. 2007; 
(b) if so, whether the matter has been inquired into, if so, the details of the findings 
and the action taken thereon; and 
(c) the compensation given by the Railways to the next of kin of the dead and to 
those seriously injured? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) In the incident of 
stampede at Mughalsarai railway station on the 3rd October, 2007; 15 persons lost 
their lives, while 12 persons sustained grievous in jury and 39 persons sustained 
simple injury.  
(b) A Committee consisting of Chief Commercial Manager (PS), Chief Medical 
Director/East Central Railway and Sr. Divisional Se curity Commissioner/Railway 
Proteetion Force, Mughalsarai/East Central Railway,  has been constituted to 
conduct enquiry into the incident. The enquiry by t he above Committee is under 
progress. 
(c) Compensation is paid only after a decree is awarded on the claim filed in this 
regard in the Railway Claims Tribunal. So far, no claim has been filed. However, the 
following amount of ex-gratia has been paid to the victims of the incident by the  
Railway Administration:— 
(i)  Rs. 15,000/- has been paid to the kins of each of the deceased persons 
after postmortem.  
(ii)  Rs. 5,000/- has been paid to each of 12 grievously injured persons.  
(iii)  Rs. 500/- has been paid to each of 39 simply injured persons.  
In addition. Hon'ble Minister for Railways has enha nced amount of ex-gratia to 
Rs. 2 lakh per head in case of death. Payment of th is enhanced ex-gratia is under 
process.  
Transplantation of Human Organs Act  
*26.   SHRI HARISH RAWAT:  
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:  
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government have made any review of the Transplantation of Human 
Organs Act, if so, the details of the outcome; and 
(b) what steps are being taken by Government to incorpo rate such outcome in 
the Act? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) and (b) A Committee was constituted by the Delhi High Court to 
review the provisions of the Transplantation of Hum an Organs Act (THOA), 1994, 
and the rules framed thereunder. After examining th e recommendations of the 
Committee, it was felt that wider consultations wit h different stakeholders were 
required. Therefore, the recommendations of the Com mittee along with the 
comments of the Ministry were placed in public domain and the  

Written Answers to  [ 19 NOV. 2007]       Starred and Unstarred Questions 99  
suggestions/comments were invited. After considerin g the responses received, a 
national consultation was conducted on 18th May, 20 07. A final review was 
organized in the Ministry in September, 2007. The general consensus that has emerged 
from the wide range of consultations is that the pr ovisions of the Transplantation of 
Human Organs Act and Rules need to be made more str ingent to deter commercial 
transactions in organ transplantation. In the asses sment of this Ministry, most of this 
can be achieved by making suitable amendments in the Rules framed under the Act. It 
has also been felt that donation of organs needs to  be popularized and encouraged 
through a National Organ Transplant Programme.  
Crop diversion to produce bio-fuels in the country  
*27. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased 
to state:  
(a) whether Government are aware that food prices are expected to remain high over 
the next decade, partly due to demand for bio-fuels  as cropping pattern changes in 
countries like US or perennial factors like massive scale floods in major parts of India 
damaging extensively standing crops; 
(b) if so, whether RBI has apprehended adverse impact o n wheat and edible oil 
prices as a consequential effect; and 
(c) what long-term measures, in co-ordination with Mini stries of Energy and 
Petroleum and National Gas, etc. are proposed to be taken so that such a situation of 
crop diversion to produce bio-fulels could be avoided? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a ) The 
Reserve Bank of India in their Mid-Term Review of A nnual Policy Statement for 
2007-08 (October, 2007) observed that food prices h ave continued to rule at 
historically high levels with no immediate relief f rom improvement in global supply 
conditions. The increase in prices has been driven by higher energy and fertilizer 
prices;low level of inventories; shortfall in certa in crops mainly caused by weather 
related factors such as the ongoing drought in Aust ralia; strong increases in the 
demand for crops particularly in growing economies of Asia and Latin America 
which are enabling their large population to spend more on foods; and change in 
cropping pattern in response to the US Governments incentives that are encouraging 
businesses to turn corn and soybeans into motor fue l. The price of com, the main 
feedstock for ethanol production in the US, rose at  the beginning of the year to ten-
year highs. As this encouraged US farmer to increas e their com production, they 
decreased the supply of other agricultural products, with a subsequent upward impact 
on the prices of these products in world markets. C onsequently, consumer price 
inflation has hardened in a number of countries, wi th food importers being most 
adversely affected.  
(b) The Reserve Bank of India in their Annual Report 2006-07 mentioned that the 
higher international prices coupled with diversion of acreage from oilseeds towards 
coarse cereals, especially maize as bio-fuel feedstock, could further exacerbate prices 
of edible oils. Further, the latest assessment of U nited States Department of 
Agriculture (USDA) mentioned that wheat apart from oilseeds is reportedly, also 
being diverted for bio-fuels. 
(c) The country has embarked on a path of bio-fuel deve lopment by utilizing the 
enormous wasteland resources. Based on the recommen dations of a Committee on 
Bio-Fuels constituted by Planning Commission, a National Mission on Bio-diesel with 
a special emphasis on plantation of jatropha has been envisaged by Ministry of Rural 
Development. Ministry of New and Renewable Energy h as formulated a draft 
National Policy on Bio-fuels which focuses on energ y security through sustainable 
production, conservation and application of bio-fue!s (Bio-diesels, 

100    Written Answers to  [RAJYA  SABHA]      Starred and Unstarred Questions  
bio-ethanol and other bio-fuels). The draft Nationa l Policy on Bio-Fuels has been 
referred to a Group of Ministers (GoM).

commodities taking into account the recommendations  of the Commission for 
Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP), the views of Central Ministries as well as such 
other relevant factors which are considered important for fixation of support prices.  
The CACP, while formulating its recommendations on price policy considers a 
number of important factors which include cost of p roduction, changes in input 
prices, input/output price parity, trends in market  prices, demand and supply

*34.   SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE:  
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA:  
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:  
(a) whether a blanket ban on junk food and colas in school and university canteens 
country wide has been proposed by his Ministry and has written to State Health 
Ministers and Vice- Chancellors of leading universi ties asking them to plan and 
implement the ban on junk food, seen as one of the main causes of the rise in heart 
disease, diabetes and cancer among India's 300- mil lion strong and increasingly 
wealthy middle class;  
(b) whether his Ministry has also communicated to the M inistry of Human 
Resource Development to finalize proposal to make h ealth and life style classes 
mandatory in schools; and 
(c) if so, the steps taken in this regard?

RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) There is no proposal to ban junk food and colas. However, 
Government is making efforts to discourage consumpt ion of junk foods including 
carbonated beverages and make people aware of nutritious and healthy foods.  
The Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare has  written to Health 
Ministers of all States and UTs and Union Minister of Human Resource 
Development to consider issuing instructions for wi thdrawal of junk food and 
carbonated drinks from school and college canteens. Letters have also been written to

Adulteration in dairy and food products  
*35.   MS. MABEL REBELLO:  
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:  
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be p leased to state:  
(a) whether Government have taken notice of the recurrent reports of the massive 
adulteration in dairy and food products in various cities; 
(b) whether Government have assessed the lacunae in existing rules and district level 
executing agencies; 
(c) if so, what steps are being taken to firm up the ex ecution of existing rules 
against adulteration; and 
(d) whether Government are considering to update th e existing measures against 
food 
adulteration; if so, the details thereof?  
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) As per information provided b y the State Food (Health) 
Authorities who are responsible for the implementat ion of the Prevention of Food 
Adulteration (PFA) Act, 1954 and Rules in their res pective StatesAJTs, the 
percentage of adulteration in samples of various fo od articles have been on the 
decline from 11.79% in 2001 to 9.57% in 2005. Of th ese samples, the average 
percentage of adulteration detected in dairy products is also found to be declining i.e. 
23.78% (2003), 21.77% (2004) and 20.68% (2005) wher eas the percentage of 
adulteration for other food products during this pe riod was 8.79% (2003), 7.58% 
(20041 and 7.88% (2005) respectively.  
Food (Health) Authorities in the States/UTs/Local b odies who implement the 
Act, have constraints like shortage of Food Inspect ors due to retirements etc., 
inadequate budgetary provisions as well as increasi ng requirements of trained 
manpower, sophisticated equipments, and reference s tandard materials in the state 
testing laboratories.  
In order to mitigate these constraints, this Ministry is implementing the World Bank 
assisted Capacity Building Project in Food and Drugs to strengthen and upgrade the 
food laboratories, including infrastructure and man power, provide training to 
enforcement staff and public analysts, etc.  
In order to keep a check on the problem of food adu lteration in the country, the 
Food (Health) authorities are advised from time to time to keep a strict vigil on the 
quality of food sold in the market by drawing food samples regularly especially of 
dairy products from all sources viz. manufacturers, vholesalers and retailers and to 
take strict action against the offenders under the provisions of the PFA Act, 1954.  
The rules made under the PFA Act are reviewed and u pdated from time to time 
wherever required. However, with the coming into fo rce of the Food Safety and 
Standards Act, 2006, the existing legal provisions for food regulation would be 
reviewed and updated wherever found necessary by the autonomous Food Authority 
provided for under the Act.

*40.   SHRI MAHMOOD A. MADANI:  
 SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:  
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:  
(a) the estimates for the deaths due to encephalitis in  the eastern part of Uttar 
Pradesh and the adjoining regions for the last three years, year-wise; 
(b) whether Government have declared it as an epidemic and if not, the reasons 
therefor; and 
(c) what steps have been taken by the Central and the S tate Governments to 
contain and mitigate the recurrent outbreak of encephalitis in certain areas? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) Japanese Encephalitis (JE) is  an outbreak prone viral 
infection having cyclic trend with seasonal phenome non. Children below 15 years 
are mostly affected. As per the report received fro m the State health authorities, the 
number of cases and deaths due to JE in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal during 
200S, 2006 and 2007 (till 02-11-07) are as under:

Government has not declared it as an epidemic as the number of deaths is lesser as 
compared to last year. However, there is a marginal increase in the number of AES/JE 
cases as compared to 2006 but much less than 2005.  
The following steps have been taken by the Central Government to contain and 
mitigate the recurrent outbreak of JE.  
Advisories have been sent alongwith standard guidel ines/protocols on AES/JE 
cases management to the State Government. Rapid Res ponse Teams have been 
formed at Districts level and have been trained. A Vector Borne Disease Surveillance 
Unit has also been established at BRD Medical Colle ge, Gorakhpur with financial 
support from Government of India for field visits a nd for strengthening of 
surveillance activities.  
To strengthen the Department of Microbiology in B.R .D. Medical College, 
Gorakhpur, one Microbiologist and one Lab Technician have been appointed out of 
Government of India funds.

The essential drugs and disposables for the management of AES/JE cases are being 
supplied to the State Government.  
Preparedness for prevention and control of AES/JE f or eastern U.P. is being 
reviewed regularly under the Chairmanship of Additi onal Director General and 
Director, National Institute of Communicable Diseases, Government of India.  
A JE vaccination campaign to cover at risk children  between 1-15 years of age 
has been launched in a phased manner from 2006. 11 districts in 4 States including 
7 districts of Uttar Pradesh and 23 districts in 10 States including 11 districts of Uttar 
Pradesh have been covered during 2006 and 2007 respectively.  
Patient with moderate to high fever with seizure are being classified and reported 
as AES cases.  
Multi-disciplinary Central teams comprising of neur ologist, epidemiologist, 
microbiologist and entomologist have been visiting the districts since August, 
2007.  
State Government/District Health Authorities are also taking following actions:  
• Daily case reporting of AES cases is being continued. 
• Treatment of AES cases is provided in the Paediatric Department, of BRD 
Medical College and district hospital, Gorakhpur. 
• AES cases and deaths are verified in the villages. 
• Line listing of the cases is being done 
• Vector control operations include fogging is being done in surrounding 
houses of confirmed J.E. cases. 
• IEC activities for prophylactic measures and early cases reporting. 
• Sero-diagnostics of the samples received from hospi tals are being carried 
out in the Microbiology Department of Gorakhpur Medical College, district 
hospital, Gorakhpur and other sentinel sites at Sid hartnagar, Basti, Deori, 
Kushi nagar, Maharajganj and Kheri.

45. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased 
to state:

(b) to what extent the NFSM helps to make the country s elf-sufficient in

KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) The Centrally Sponsor ed Scheme National 
Food Security Mission (NFSM) has been launched with  the objectives to increase 
the production of rice, wheat and pulses in the ide ntified district of the country by 
10, 8 and 2 million tonnes, respectively by the end of Eleventh Plan (2011-12) so as to 
achieve self-sufficiency in foodgrains production.  
(c) National Food Security Mission (NFSM) has three com ponents viz. National 
Food Security Mission-Rice (NFSM-Rice), National Fo od Security Mission-Wheat 
(NFSM-Wheat) and National Food Security Mission-Pul ses (NFSM-Pulses). The 
interventions included under NFSM are demonstration s on improved production 
technologies; distribution of quality seeds of high  yielding varieties & hybrids; 
popularization of newly released varieties through seed minikits; support for micro-
nutrients, gypsum, zero tillage, rotavators, conoweeders and other farm implements, 
integrated pest management, integrated nutrient man agement; water lifting and 
moisture saving device; training and mass media campaign including award for best 
performing districts etc. Besides, the pilot projec ts on community generators, 
management of blue bulls and demonstrations of Inte rnational Crop Research 
Institute for Semi Arid Tropics (ICRISAT) technolog ies are also included. The 
identified districts are given flexibility to adopt  the area specific technological 
interventions suited to their local conditions.

Statement-II  
Details of steps taken by Government for the prevention of DENGUE, AIDS, TB And 
Leprosy  
In respect of Dengue, Government of India has prepa red a Long Term Action 
Plan for prevention and control the disease in the country and sent to the States for 
implementation. 110 Sentinel Surveillance Hospitals (SSHs) have been identified in 
the country for proactive surveillance. These Sentinel Surveillance Hospitals are linked 
with 13 Apex Referral Laboratories for Quality Assu rance, capacity building and 
backup support. Microbiologists and laboratory tech nicians of the SSHs have been 
trained on sero-diagnosis at Apex Referral Laboratories. NIV, Pune has been entrusted 
to supply IgM ELISA test kits for diagnosis of Deng ue to the identified institutes. 
Guidelines for clinical management of Dengue/DHF cases have been sent to the States 
for wider circulation. Adulticides and larvicides as per technical requirement of States 
are being supplied. Advisories are issued from time to time. Periodic review is done 
to monitor the status at higher level. Central team s are sent for investigation of 
outbreak and to provide technical guidance to the States.  
In respect of AIDS, Government of India is implemen ting the National AIDS 
Control Programme as a 100% Centrally sponsored sch eme. The strategy is based 
primarily on preventing new infections by focused i nterventions among high risk 
groups and also providing care, support and treatme nt to HIV infected persons. For 
increasing awareness about and creating demand gene ration for services, emphasis 
is placed on IEC through mass media channels and in ter-personal communications. 
Government of India has launched National AIDS Cont rol Programme phase III 
with the goal to halt and reverse the epidemic, in the country over the next 5 years 
by integrating programmes for prevention, care, sup port and treatment. This will be 
achieved through a four-pronged strategy:  
(i) Prevention of new infections in high risk groups and general population.  
(ii)  Providing greater care, support and treatment to larger number of PLHA.  
(iii)  Strengthening the infrastructure, systems and human resources in 
prevention, care, support and treatment programmes at the District, State 
and National leveL  
(iv) Strengthening the nationwide Strategic Information Management System.  
In respect of Leprosy, Government of India is implementing the National Leprosy 
Eradication Programme since year 1983-1984 with the aim to eliminate leprosy as a 
public health problem at National level. The countr y achieved elimination in 
December, 2005. For prevention & control of the dis ease, the following steps are 
being followed:  

Written Answers to  [19 NOV. 2007]     Starred and Unstarred Questions 127 
 
• Integration of NLEP services with the General Health Care system. 
• Capacity building of primary health care functionaries in management of 
leprosy cases. 
• Timely diagnosis & prompt treatment with Multi Drug Theraphy (MDT). 
• Intensified Information, Education & Communication (IEC) using Local 
and Mass Media. 
• Prevention of Disability & Medical Rehabilitation. 
• Monitoring & Evaluation through Management Information System and 
Independent Evaluation. 
 
In respect of TB, the Revised National TB Control P rogramme (RNTCP) widely 
known as DOTS, which is WHO recommended strategy, i s being implemented as a 
100% Centrally Sponsored Scheme from 1997 in the co untry in a phased manner 
with an objective to achieve cure rate of 85% of ne w sputum positive cases and to 
detect at least 70% of such cases. By March 23,2006 , all the districts in the country 
are implementing RNTCP, allowing access of DOTS to all TB patients in the 
country. Under the programme, diagnosis and treatme nt facilities including a 
supply of anti TB drugs are provided free of cast t o all TB patients. For quality 
diagnosis, designated microscopy centres have been established for every one lac 
population in the normal areas and for every 50,000  population in the tribal, hilly 
and difficult areas. Sputum microscopy instead of X -ray avoids over diagnosis and 
identified infectious cases. More than 12250 micros copy centres have been 
established in the country. Drugs are provided to t he TB patients in patient wise 
boxes to ensure that all durgs for full course of t reatment are earmarked the day one 
a patient is registered for treatment under the pro gramme. Treatment centres (DOT 
centres) have been established near to residence of  patients to the extent possible. 
All Government hospitals, Community Health Centres (CHC), Primary Health 
Centres (PHCs), Sub-centres are DOT Centres, in add ition, NGOs, Private 
Practitioners (PPs) involved under the RNTCP, Commu nity Volunteers, 
Anganwadi workers, Women Self Groups etc. also func tion as DOT 
Providers/DOT Centres. Drugs are provided under dir ect observation and the 
patients are monitored so that they complete their treatment.  
 
To improve quality of services, full requirement of  Anti-TB drugs and 
Binocular Microscopes are supplied by the Centre to  the States as commodity 
grant. For undertaking various activities for imple mentation of RNTCP in the 
State, funds as grants-in-aid are provided by the C entre to the State Health 
Societies for onward transmission to Districts. Sta te TB Cells and District TB 
Centres have been strengthened by providing key per sonnel on contract basis and 
necessary infrastructure such as four wheelers, two  wheelers, fax machine, 
photocopier, computer and internet facilities. All the State TB Cells and District 
TB Centres of the country are connected electronica lly and reports are received 
through internet. For supervision of microscopy cen tres and DOT centres, at the 
sub-district level a TB Units (TUs) have been set u p at sub-district level for every 
five lakh population (for 2.5 lakh people in tribal  and hilly areas). At the TU level 
one Senior Treatment Supervisor (STS) and one Senio r Tuberculosis Laboratory 
Supervisor (STLS) have been provided on contractual  basis who work under 
designated Medical Officer TB Control (MOTC) respon sible for all TB control 
activities at sub-district level.  
 
To make the programme more accessible to larger seg ments of the population, 
and to supplement the Government efforts in this di rection, emphasis is being 
given to also involve medical colleges, all general  hospitals, Corporate hospitals, 
private practitioners and NGOs in the programme.

are brought to the notice by the beneficiaries, the  hospitals are liable for liquidated 
damages to be deducted from the performance bank guarantee submitted by the concerned 
hospital/diagnostic centre. In case of repeated instances of defaults, the total amount of 
bank guarantee may be forfeited and also result in termination of MOA.

continuous process. Any private hospital/diagnostic centres may apply to the CGHS if

Maternal mortality in Orissa  
64. MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: Will the Minister of HEALT H AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state:  
(a) whether it is a fact that the country faces a f ormidable challenge on maternal 
mortality, which shows that tens of thousands of malnourished, health-poor and resource-
poor women without access to hospitals, continue to die during pregnancy while giving 
birth, etc.;  

130    Written Answers to  [RAJYASABHA]     Starred and Unstarred Questions  
(b) what is the status of this menace in the country, especially with reference to Orissa State; 
and 
(c) what is the action of the Centre to help Orissa State both physically and financially to 
control this menace? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Based on the official estimates of Registrar General 
of India (RGI), Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) for India is 301 per 100,000 live births (SRS 
2001—03). This translates into an absolute number of maternal deaths of approximately 77,000 
per year.  
The same report lists, the causes of maternal deaths in the county as—Hemorrhage—38%, 
Sepsis—11%, Abortion —8%, Obstructed Labour—5%, Hypertensive Disorders—5% and 
Others—34%. Causes classified as Others" include Anemia and Malnutrition. Factors like low 
socio-economic status, lack of access to services and poverty are said to contribute to maternal 
mortality.  
(b) MMR for India and other major States including Orissa are enclosed as Statement. (See 
below) 
(c) The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) launched by the Government of India in 
the year 2005, in order to improve the availability of and access to quality health care including 
services for Immunization and Safe Motherhood, seeks to provide effective health care to rural 
population throughout the country with special focus on 18 States with weak public health 
indicators and/or weak infrastructure, which also includes Orissa. 
In order to bring about a reduction in MMR, the Government of India is implementing the 
following key interventions all over the country including the State of Orissa which include: 
Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) a cash benefit scheme to promote Institutional Delivery with a 
special focus on Below Poverty Line (BPL and SC/ST pregnant women; Appointment of an 
Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) for every village to facilitate in accessing of health 
care services by the community including pregnant women; operationalizing Community 
Health Centers as First Referral Units (FRU) and 50% of all Primary Health Centers for 
providing 24X7 delivery services by 2010; augmenting the availability of Skilled Manpower 
by means of different skill based trainings such as Skilled Birth Attendant, Training of MBBS 
Doctors in Life Saving Anesthetic Skills and Emergency Obstetric Care including Caesarian 
Section; prevention and treatment of Anemia by supplementation with Iron and Folic Acid 
tablets; organizing of Village Health & Nutrition Day at Anganwadi center; supplementary 
nutrition to pregnant and lactating women under the ICDS scheme and strengthening of sub-
centers by providing each with an untied fund of Rs. 10, 000/- to improve service delivery.  
Under NRHM and RCH II financial resources are allocated to the States, by the Centre 
through flexible funding mechanisms, whereby the States have the flexibility to plan and implement 
strategies and interventions as per their requirement and priorities.  
During 2006-07, and amount of Rs. 60.01 crores was released to Orissa and during 2007-08 
Rs. 41.59 crores has been released so far.

66. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:  
(a) whether the country is facing an acute shortage of nurses and if so, the reasons 
therefor, 
(b) the actual number of nurses registered in the country as on the 1 st November, 2007 
and the number out of them who are actually active in the profession; 
(c) names of the States which are particularly affected by shortage of nurses; and 
(d) what effective steps are proposed to remedy the situation and by when the country 
is expected to achieve self sufficiency in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (c) As  per the Bajaj 
Committee recommendations of Nurses patient ratio, 10.43 lakhs Nurses would be 
required by 2012. With the existing strength of live Nurses and the training capacity, 
6.84 lakhs Nurses would be available by 2012. It means that there will be a shortage of 
3.59 lakhs by 2012. This gap will be mostly in the States of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya 
Pradesh, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jammu and Kashmir, Jharkhand and Orissa.  
(b) Total number of Nurses registered to various State Nursing Councils is 9.28 lakhs. 
There is no Live Register of Nurses with the State Nursing Councils. It is estimated that 
only 40% of Nurses are active.

maintenance practices, Modernisation of Bridge Mana gement System, Signaling

80. SHRI B.J. PANDA:  
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR:  
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state:  
(a) whether in order to control rail accidents, it is p roposed to construct subways 
at crossings, build road over-bridges and convert u nmanned level crossings into 
manned ones; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the details of construction of such subways, road o ver-bridges and manned 
level crosssings on the EcoR system? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS ( SHRI R. 
VELU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. In order to control ra il accidents at unmanned level 
crossings (UMLC) it has been proposed to construct limited use subways wherever 
height of embankment makes it feasible. Till now 444 sites have been identified out 
of which 312 have already been sanctioned.  
Further, the conversion of UMLCs to manned ones is based on the traffic 
volume and visibility conditions. There are 632 unm anned level crossings meeting 
the criteria of manning, out of which 477 have been targeted for manning in 2007-08. 
Additionally, in order to ensure safe, smooth and s ecure flow of both rail and road 
traffic, railways construct road over/under bridges (ROB/RUB) on cost sharing basis 
with the State Governments if the traffic density i n terms of Train Vehicle 
Units(TVU-A unit obtained by multiplying the number of trains with the number of 
road vehicles passing over the level crossing in 24 hours) exceeds the prescribed norm 
of 1 lakh, or otherwise on deposit terms. ROB/RUB a re also encouraged on Build 
Own and Transfer (BOT) concept. At present, there a re 582 works of ROB/RUB 
sanctioned on cost sharing basis, 141 on Deposit te rms and 54 on BOT concept. In 
addition 225 works are being constructed by Nationa l Highway Authority of India 
(NHAI).  
(c) On East Coast Railway there are no unmanned lev el crossings meeting the 
criteria of manning at Railway cost. However, 16 wo rks of ROB/RUB have been 
sanctioned on cost sharing basis, 5 of which are targeted for completion during 2007-
08.96 limited height subways have been identified on this Railway. 2 works of ROB 
are being executed by NHAI on this Railway.

*1. SHRI VARINDER SINGH BAJWA: Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS

(a) whether Government have formulated a new sports policy taking into consideration 
the poor infrastructure for the development of Indian sports, particularly hockey, football,

Panchayati Raj institutions and SHGs  
* 11. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of PANCHAYATI RAJ be pleased 
to state:  
(a) whether Government are evolving a scheme, with co-operation of World Bank for 
federating self-help groups (SHGs) into Panchayati Raj institutions to organize 
women from poor and disadvantaged rural households to make them vibrant and 
self-sufficient; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) whether Government have developed any mechanism to periodically monitor 
working of Panchayati Raj outfits? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANI SHANKAR A IYAR): 
(a) At present, there is no such proposal under the  consideration of the Ministry of 
Panchayati Raj.  
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) The first task before the Ministry was to evolve a national consensus in 
respect of the Roadmap for Panchayati Raj through mutual consultation between the 
Centre and the States. Ministry of Panchayati Raj convened Seven Round Tables of 
State Panchayati Raj Ministers with the Union Minis ter of Panchayati Raj between 
July and December 2004. The deliberations centered on the 18 identified dimensions of 
Panchayati Raj ranging from the effective Devolution of the Functions, Finances and 
Functionaries to District Planning, Training and Capacity Building and IT-enabled e-
governance. At the conclusion of each Round Table, nearly 150 action points 
comprised in the Compendium were unanimously adopte d by all Panchayati Raj 
Ministers and referred to Chief Ministers for their  approval. This has become a 
National Roadmap for effective Panchayati Raj. Further, the Minister (Panchayati Raj) 
has visited 23 States and Union Territories and sig ned a joint declaration with the 
respective Chief Ministers of States setting forth the path to full empowerment of 
Panchayats. 
The Ministry of Panchayati Raj is continually inter acting with the State 
Governments to ascertain the effectiveness of PRIs. A Committee of Panchayati Raj 
Secretaries was constituted to monitor the progress and implementation of these 150 
Action Points. This Committee of Secretaries headed  by the Secretary, Ministry of 
Panchayati Raj would also service the Council of Pa nchayati Raj Ministers. The 
Committee of Secretaries has held nine meetings. The Council of Ministers has been 
convened thrice, at Kochi, Kerala in August 2005, at Bhubaneswar, Orissa in June 2006 
and at Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala in August 2007, r espectively. The Empowered 
Sub-Committee of National Development Council also reviews the progress of 
implementation of the provision of the Constitution  during its meetings, which are 
held periodically. Most of these action points revolve around follow up measures on 
activity mapping, matching transfer of funds and functionaries, creation of Panchayat 
sector in the State budget, constitution and operat ional guidelines for the District 
Planning Committees within an agreed time-frame.

Noise levels of crackers  
16. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be  pleased to 
state:  
(a) whether is it a fact that manufacturers of crackers  are required by law to print 
the noise level on the boxes of crackers being sold in the market; 
(b) whether is it also a fact that 90 per cent crackers fait to clear prescribed noise level 
norms; 
(c) if so, the action that has been taken by Government  against cracker 
manufacturers and how many have been charged under the law; 
(d) whether Central Pollution Control Board has conduct ed any enquiry into the 
matter and any raids conducted; and 
(e) the steps Government have taken to reduce noise and air pollution during festive 
seasons likeDiwali? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMEN T AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (d) The Mi nistry of 
Environment and Forests has notified the noise leve ls for firecrackers in October, 
1999 under the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986 . As per information provided 
by the Central Pollution Control Board, the testing  results of the samples of 
firecrackers tested during last three years have in dicated about 75% having failed to 
comply with the prescribed noise levels. With respect to the firecrackers, the Hon'ble 
Supreme Court, in its Order of July 2005, in the ma tter of Noise Pollution has, inter 
alia, observed that between the present system of evaluating firecrackers on the basis 
of noise levels, and the other where the firecracke rs are evaluated on the basis of 
chemical composition, the later method is more prac tical and workable in Indian 
circumstances and it shall be followed unless and u ntil replaced by a better system. 
Further, that the Department of Explosives shall un dertake necessary research 
activities for the purpose and come out with the ch emical formulae for each type of 
cracker or class of firecrackers. It is also mentio ned in the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
Order that every manufacturer shall, on the box of each firecracker, mention details of 
its chemical contents and that it satisfies the req uirement as laid down by the 
Department of Explosives.  
In pursuance to the aforesaid Order of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the 
Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (Forme rly-Department of 
Explosives) has already initiated a study to decide  on the chemical composition of 
fire crackers to comply with noise standards.

Death of leopards  
17. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state:  
(a) whether it is a fact that in 100 days from June 1,2007 to September 10,2007,14 
leopards died in various parts of the country for various reasons, thereby endangering the 
species; 
(b) if so, the number of leopards presently living in the country (as on 31.10.07) as 
compared to their number of 8203, according to the census in 2001-02; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to protect the animal from extinction? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMEN T AND 
FORESTS (SHRI S. REGUPATHY): (a) As per the informa tion received from the 
State/UT Governments, there are reports of death of leopards due to various reasons in 
different parts of the country.  
(b) No population estimation of leopards is available after 2001-02 for comparison. 
(c) The measures taken by Government of India to ensure protection of leopards, inter 
alia, include the following: 
 
1. Leopard has been included in the Schedule I of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 
1972, thus according them the highest degree of protection. 
2. A network of National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries has been set up across 
the country to protect wildlife including leopards. 
3. Wildlife Crime Control Bureau, with a network of five Regional and three Sub 
Regional Offices, has been set upto control wildlife crimes. 
4. Financial support is being provided under the Centrally Sponsored Schemes-
Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries, Project Tiger and Project 
Elephant, to State/UT Governments for the conservation and development of 
wildlife and its habitats. 
5. India is a signatory to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species 
of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) that regulates international trade in wildlife 
and its derivatives. 
In addition, the State/UT Governments have also taken the following measures to 
protect wild animals including leopards:  
1. Development of wildlife habitat to increase the population of wild animals. 
2. Intensive patrolling in sensitive areas. 
3. Deployment of Ex-service men for patrolling.

(a) the present status with regard to the implementation of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 
1995; 
(b) the steps taken by Government during the preceding two years in the direction; 
(c) Government's viewpoint on the implementation or otherwise on this legislation; 
and 
(d) the manner in which Government propose to balance the interest of both the landlord 
and tenant at least in the case of new tenancies in Delhi? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI AJAY MAKEN): (a) to (d) Immediately after The Delhi Rent Act, 1995 was 
enacted on 23.8.1995 there were representations against some of the provisions of the said 
Act by a section of tenants. The matter was examined and it was decided to bring the Act 
into force after effecting amendments to some of its provisions.  
The Delhi Rent (Amendment) Bill, 1997 was accordingly introduced in Rajya Sabha in 
July, 1997. The Bill could not be debated till the dissolution of the. 13th Lok Sabha. After 
formation of 14th Lok Sabha, the bill is required to be considered by the Government afresh 
and steps have been initiated in that direction.  
It is expected that after the Delhi Rent (Amendment) Bill is passed and brought into 
force, the observed deficiencies in The Delhi Rent Act, 1995 would be removed since 
provisions have been made in the Bill to balance the interest of both the landlord and 
tenant.

Statement-II  
Steps taken by Centre to speed up implementation of  projects/reforms under JNNURM 
for States which have lagged behind  
Efforts being made by the Centre to speed up implementation of projects/reforms 
under JNNURM for States which have lagged behind include:—  
(i) Periodic reviews by Central Sanctioning and Monitoring Committee (CSMC).  
(ii)  Regional Review Meetings.  
(iii)  Monthly D.O. letters from Secretary (UD) to Chief Secretaries of States.  
(iv)  Day to day interaction with States.  
(v) In-depth review of implementation of Reforms at  State and City levels by 
Reform Appraisal Agencies.  
(vi) Support to establish program Management Unit ( PMU) at State Level Nodal 
Agencies (SLNA) level to accelerate implementation of reforms, enhance the 
quality of physical works and improve efficiency in service delivery.  
(vii) Extending financial and technical support to establish Project Implementation 
Units (PIUs) at Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) to enhance their capability to effectively 
implement projects and reforms under JNNURM.  
(viii) Third party monitoring and review of the projects sanctioned under the JNNURM 
through appointment of Independent Review and Monitoring Agencies (IRMAs).  
(ix) An indicative list of organisations has been c ompiled, based on the relevant 
technical parameters, and circulated to State Governments and Urban Local Bodies 
(ULBs) to facilitate the preparation of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs).  
(x) Capacity Building and Communication activities through Rapid Training Program 
(RTP), Peer Experience and Reflective Learning (PEARL) to foster cross learning 
among cities and institutions.  
(xi)  Award to cities and States that perform well in implementation of the Mission,  
(xii)  Communication Campaign,  
(xiii)  Engagement of Civil Society,  
(xiv)  Community Participation Fund (CPF).  
(xv)  Credit Rating of Urban Land Bodies.  
(xvi)  Municipal Finance Improvement Programme (MFIP).  
(xvii)  Pooled Finance Development Fund.

devastating cyclone which has taken place in our neighbouring country Bangladesh. I 
requested the Leader of the Opposition also and he has readily agreed that I could 
make this statement.  
Sir, I rise to inform the House about the recent cy clone and devastation which 
has been caused in neighbouring Bangladesh. As hon.  Members would be aware, a 
severe cyclone hit Bangladesh, especially its coast al districts, on 15th November 
causing in its wake death and devastation. More tha n 2,300 persons are reported 
dead, as of now, and several thousands rendered homeless. An estimated 2.7 million 
people have also been affected; thousands of livest ock are killed and standing crops 
and infrastructure are severely damaged.  
Rashtrapatiji and the hon. Prime Minister have writ ten to their counterparts in 
Bangladesh expressing our distress at this tragedy and conveying our deep 
condolences and our readiness to assist them in the  relief efforts. Yesterday, I had 
spoken to Dr. Iftekhar Ahmed Chowdury, Foreign Advi ser to the Caretaker 
Government of Bangladesh, and mentioned to him our readiness to send relief 
supplies to supplement the efforts of the Government of Bangladesh.  
As Bangladesh struggles to come to terms with this devastation, in keeping with our 
close ties and our empathy with the friendly people of Bangladesh in this hour of need, 
the Government of India has decided to respond imme diately with a comprehensive 
relief package. Our offer will consist of relief ma terials required urgently by those 
affected. This package will consist of medicines, food items, milk powder, tents and 
blankets, first-aid kits and other relief items.  
The hon. Members will recollect that India has always responded readily to such 
requests from Bangladesh earlier, the most recent one being a few months ago when 
considerable devastation was caused by mudslides du ring the monsoons. We are 
already in the process of supplying essential food items to Bangladesh. We will 
continue to extend whatever assistance we can this time as well. Thank you, Sir.
